items.prompt: How does a jellyfish sting something that brushes against its tentacles?

options.label: Coiled, thread-like darts fire out on contact
options.feedback: Held inside a tiny capsule under pressure, this coiled thread shoots outward the instant it is touched, piercing and injecting venom.

options.label: It bites down with small hidden teeth
options.feedback: A jellyfish's tentacles carry no teeth at all; the sting comes from a completely different kind of structure.

options.label: Acid on its skin burns on contact
options.feedback: No acid coats a jellyfish's tentacles; the harm instead comes from a venom injected mechanically, not by surface chemistry.

options.label: It sprays venom into the surrounding water
options.feedback: The venom is not sprayed loose into the water; it only reaches a target through direct contact with the tentacle.

items.ok_line: A tiny coiled thread, fired the instant something brushes against it.
items.ko_line: Think about what could be coiled up tightly and ready to shoot outward at the lightest touch.
items.exp_title: A coiled thread waiting to fire
items.exp_text: Scattered across a jellyfish's tentacles are countless tiny capsules called nematocysts, each holding a coiled, hollow thread under great internal pressure. The moment something brushes against a trigger on the capsule's surface, the thread shoots outward and turns inside out as it fires, piercing the target and injecting venom in a fraction of a second. Because each capsule fires independently and only once, a tentacle that has just stung something is left with many of its threads already spent.

items.prompt: A jellyfish has no brain. How does it manage to coordinate the pulsing movements of its bell?

options.label: A net of nerve cells spread through its body coordinates the pulse
options.feedback: Spread evenly across the body rather than gathered into one place, this net of connected nerve cells fires in a coordinated rhythm.

options.label: Each part of its body moves entirely on its own, with no coordination
options.feedback: The pulses of a jellyfish's bell are in fact well coordinated, spreading evenly rather than moving randomly or independently.

options.label: It relies on a single nerve running down its centre, much like a spine
options.feedback: There is no central nerve cord running through a jellyfish's body; its nerve cells are instead spread out in a loose, even net.

options.label: Muscles in the bell contract at random, and the pulse only looks coordinated
options.feedback: The rhythm is not an illusion produced by randomness; a connected net of nerve cells actively coordinates each pulse.

items.ok_line: No single control centre, just nerve cells spread out and working together.
items.ko_line: Think about coordination that comes from a web spread through the whole body, rather than from one central point.
items.exp_title: A web of nerves instead of a brain
items.exp_text: Rather than a brain, a jellyfish has a loose, even net of nerve cells spread through its bell and connected to one another at many points. A signal starting anywhere in this net spreads outward in every direction, reaching the muscles of the bell at close to the same moment and triggering them to contract together. That shared timing is what produces the smooth, rhythmic pulse of the bell, even without any single structure directing it.

items.prompt: How does a coral polyp actually build the hard, rock-like structure of a reef?

options.label: It secretes a hard skeleton of calcium carbonate beneath itself
options.feedback: Drawn from dissolved minerals in the surrounding seawater, this material is laid down as a hard cup, and generations of polyps build layer upon layer over it.

options.label: It cements together loose shells and sand
options.feedback: A reef is not simply cemented from stray debris; the hard structure is actively produced by the polyps' own bodies, mineral by mineral.

options.label: It weaves together strands of dried algae
options.feedback: Algae live closely with coral, but the reef's hard structure is not woven from any plant material at all.

options.label: It hardens its own soft body permanently into stone
options.feedback: The polyp's own soft body stays soft and living; the hard structure is a separate skeleton built and left beneath it.

items.ok_line: Mineral drawn from seawater, laid down again and again beneath a living polyp.
items.ko_line: Think about a mineral the polyp could pull from the water around it and lay down as a hard base.
items.exp_title: Stone built by a soft animal
items.exp_text: A coral polyp is a small, soft-bodied animal that draws dissolved calcium and carbonate straight out of the surrounding seawater and combines them into a hard mineral, which it deposits as a cup-shaped skeleton beneath its own body. As the polyp grows, it adds fresh mineral to the rim of that cup, and neighbouring polyps in the same colony do the same side by side. Over long stretches of time, the skeletons left behind by countless polyps, generation after generation, build up into the solid structure of a reef.

items.prompt: Why does most reef-building coral rely so heavily on tiny algae living inside its own tissue?

options.label: The algae photosynthesise and share their sugars with the coral
options.feedback: Sheltered inside the coral's tissue and given sunlight, the algae make sugar through photosynthesis and pass much of it directly to their host.

options.label: The algae dissolve rock to release minerals for the coral
options.feedback: The algae's role is producing food through photosynthesis, not dissolving rock to free up minerals for their coral host.

options.label: The algae camouflage the coral from predators
options.feedback: It is the algae's photosynthesis, not any camouflaging effect, that explains why the coral depends on them so heavily.

options.label: The algae filter parasites out of the coral's tissue
options.feedback: Filtering parasites is not the algae's function; their value to the coral comes from the food they produce through photosynthesis.

items.ok_line: A steady supply of food, made from sunlight, delivered from just inside its own tissue.
items.ko_line: Think about what living inside sunlit water would let a tiny alga actually make.
items.exp_title: A tenant that pays in food
items.exp_text: Living inside a coral polyp's own tissue are millions of tiny algae, sheltered from predators and bathed in the sunlight that filters down through shallow water. Using that sunlight, the algae photosynthesise and produce far more sugar than they themselves need, passing much of the surplus directly to the coral that houses them. In return for that steady, built-in food supply, the coral provides the algae with a safe, sunlit place to live and with certain nutrients drawn from its own waste.

items.prompt: What actually happens to a coral when it "bleaches" and loses its colour?

options.label: Stressed, it expels the coloured algae living inside its tissue
options.feedback: Since most of the coral's colour comes from those algae, driving them out under stress leaves the coral's pale, white skeleton showing through.

options.label: Sunlight directly burns away the coral's own pigment
options.feedback: It is not the coral's own pigment being burned away directly; the pale colour appears because the coloured algae inside it are expelled.

options.label: A fungus grows over the coral and turns it white
options.feedback: No fungus is involved in this whitening; the cause lies in the coral's own tissue losing the algae that normally colour it.

options.label: The coral's skeleton itself changes colour with age
options.feedback: The mineral skeleton underneath was already pale to begin with; bleaching is about the loss of colour from the living tissue on top of it.

items.ok_line: The colour was never the coral's own; losing it exposes the white beneath.
items.ko_line: Remember where most of a healthy coral's colour actually comes from.
items.exp_title: Losing a tenant, and its colour along with it
items.exp_text: Most of a coral's colour comes not from its own tissue but from the algae living inside it, and when the coral is placed under stress, such as unusually warm water, it can expel those algae from its tissue. Without the algae, the coral's own tissue turns out to be nearly transparent, and the pale white of its mineral skeleton shows straight through from underneath. Left without its main food source for too long after this, a bleached coral can eventually starve.

items.prompt: A jellyfish has no fins or strong swimming muscles like a fish. How does it manage to stay afloat and move through the water?

options.label: A watery, jelly-like body gives it near-neutral buoyancy, and its bell pulses to move
options.feedback: Made almost entirely of water held within a jelly-like layer, its body weighs about the same as the surrounding seawater, and rhythmic pulses of the bell push it along.

options.label: It clings to floating debris to stay near the surface
options.feedback: A jellyfish does not depend on drifting objects to stay afloat; its buoyancy comes from its own watery body.

options.label: Gas trapped inside its bell keeps it afloat
options.feedback: There is no pocket of trapped gas inside a jellyfish's bell; its ability to float comes from how watery its tissue is, not from any gas.

options.label: It stays permanently attached to the seafloor
options.feedback: Most jellyfish drift freely through open water for most of their lives rather than staying fixed to the seafloor.

items.ok_line: A body built almost entirely from water, pulsed gently along rather than fought against.
items.ko_line: Think about what a jellyfish's body is mostly made of, and how that would compare in weight to the water around it.
items.exp_title: A body that barely weighs more than water
items.exp_text: A jellyfish's bell is filled with a soft, jelly-like layer called mesoglea that is made up overwhelmingly of water, so the whole body weighs very close to the same as the seawater surrounding it. Because it is already close to neutrally buoyant, the jellyfish does not need strong muscle to stay afloat, only enough to control its position. Rhythmic contractions of the bell squeeze water out from underneath it, pushing the jellyfish gently forward with each pulse.

items.prompt: A jellyfish has no separate stomach and no separate opening for waste. How does it manage to digest a meal?

options.label: A single central cavity serves as both mouth and digestive space
options.feedback: Food enters this cavity through the very same opening used afterward to expel whatever is left undigested.

options.label: It digests food entirely outside its body before swallowing it
options.feedback: Digestion in a jellyfish happens inside a body cavity, not out in the open water before anything is swallowed.

options.label: It absorbs food directly through its outer skin
options.feedback: Food is drawn in through a central opening into an inner cavity, not absorbed directly through the outer surface of the body.

options.label: Special bacteria inside its tentacles do the digesting for it
options.feedback: No bacteria housed in the tentacles are responsible for digestion; that happens within the jellyfish's own central body cavity.

items.ok_line: One opening, doing the work that two separate ones do in most other animals.
items.ko_line: Think about a body plan simple enough to need only a single opening for everything.
items.exp_title: One opening for both ends of the job
items.exp_text: A jellyfish's body is built around a single central cavity, and food captured by the tentacles is passed through one opening into that cavity, where it is broken down and its nutrients absorbed. Whatever cannot be digested is then expelled back out through that very same opening, since no second, separate opening exists for waste. This simple, single-entrance body plan is shared by the jellyfish's close relatives, including sea anemones and coral polyps.

items.prompt: How does a sea anemone catch prey swimming past its waving tentacles?

options.label: Its tentacles fire stinging cells to paralyse the prey, then draw it in
options.feedback: Once the venom has stopped the prey's struggling, the tentacles curl inward and guide the catch toward the mouth at the centre.

options.label: It traps prey in a sticky mucus web spread across the seafloor
options.feedback: No web of mucus is spread out to trap prey; the capture instead relies on stinging cells firing directly from the tentacles.

options.label: It sucks in nearby water violently to pull prey inward
options.feedback: There is no strong inward suction used to draw prey in; capture instead depends on the sting delivered by the tentacles themselves.

options.label: It waits for prey to die naturally nearby before eating it
options.feedback: A sea anemone actively subdues live prey using its stinging tentacles rather than simply waiting to scavenge creatures that happen to die close by.

items.ok_line: A sting first, then tentacles that curl the catch straight toward the mouth.
items.ko_line: Think about what a sea anemone's tentacles have in common with a jellyfish's.
items.exp_text: A sea anemone's tentacles are lined with the same kind of stinging cells found on a jellyfish, each ready to fire a venomous barb into anything that brushes against it. Small fish or invertebrates swimming too close are stung and quickly subdued, and the surrounding tentacles then curl inward, drawing the paralysed prey toward the mouth at the centre of the anemone's body. Prey too large or too strong to subdue this way is usually left alone, since the sting works best against smaller, weaker animals.

items.prompt: Why doesn't a clownfish get stung when it hides among the tentacles of a sea anemone?

options.label: A coating of mucus on its skin keeps the anemone's stinging cells from firing
options.feedback: Built up gradually as the clownfish rubs against the tentacles, this mucus coating stops the anemone from recognising it as prey worth stinging.

options.label: The clownfish's scales are too thick for the sting to pierce
options.feedback: Thickness of the scales is not what protects a clownfish; the anemone's sting is stopped from firing at all, thanks to a coating on the skin.

options.label: The anemone recognises the clownfish and never fires at any fish
options.feedback: An anemone will readily sting most other fish that touch its tentacles; the clownfish's protection is not a general rule about all fish.

options.label: The clownfish is immune to any amount of the venom itself
options.feedback: The protection works by stopping the sting from firing in the first place, not by the clownfish tolerating venom that reaches it.

items.ok_line: A coating that keeps the anemone's stinging cells from ever firing at all.
items.ko_line: Think about what could stop the trigger on a stinging cell from firing in the first place.
items.exp_title: A coat that hides it from the sting
items.exp_text: A clownfish gradually builds up a layer of mucus on its skin by rubbing gently against the anemone's tentacles over repeated contact, and that mucus appears to keep the anemone's stinging cells from recognising it as something worth firing at. Protected this way, the clownfish can dart freely in and out of the tentacles that would sting almost any other fish that touched them, using the anemone as a safe shelter from predators. In turn, the clownfish often chases off other fish that might otherwise nibble at the anemone.

items.prompt: Many coral polyps stay hidden by day and only extend their tentacles at night. Why?

options.label: Darkness is when the plankton they feed on drifts within reach
options.feedback: With plankton rising and drifting closer after dark, extending the tentacles at night lets the polyp catch far more food than it would by day.

options.label: Sunlight would burn their soft tentacles
options.feedback: Coral tissue can withstand daytime sunlight without harm, so avoiding a burn is not the reason the tentacles stay retracted.

options.label: Predators can only see the tentacles in daylight
options.feedback: Many predators of coral polyps hunt just as effectively after dark, so simply avoiding daytime sight is not the main reason.

options.label: Cooler night-time water helps the tentacles capture prey better
options.feedback: Water temperature is not what changes the tentacles' effectiveness at capturing prey; the real difference at night is where the food itself is.

items.ok_line: Tentacles out when the food itself is close enough to catch.
items.ko_line: Think about what changes in the water around a reef once the sun goes down.
items.exp_title: Reaching out when the food arrives
items.exp_text: Many small drifting animals that make up plankton spend daylight hours lower in the water or hidden away, only rising closer to the reef once darkness falls. A coral polyp gains little by keeping its soft, vulnerable tentacles extended during the day, when this main food source is scarce near the surface of the reef. Once night brings the plankton within reach, the polyp extends its tentacles and begins catching prey drifting past.
